articles.title: The Wings Folded Inside
articles.dek: In 1668 a young Dutch naturalist peeled back a caterpillar's skin and found a butterfly already waiting there. John saw the same hidden future in the children of God.
articles.quote: What God will make of you is already folded inside you, and he has never once lost track of it.
articles.body:
In 1668, a visiting prince from Florence named Cosimo de' Medici sat down in an Amsterdam workroom to watch a demonstration he would talk about for years. His host was Jan Swammerdam, a thin, intense young man of thirty-one, the son of an apothecary, who had spent his youth collecting insects when other boys were learning their fathers' trade. In those days most learned people believed that a caterpillar and a butterfly were two different creatures, and that in the chrysalis one simply died and another was conjured in its place. Swammerdam had come to doubt it. He took a caterpillar near the time of its change, and with instruments so fine he ground some of them himself, he gently drew back its skin. There, folded tight against the body like a letter in an envelope, lay the wings, the legs, and the long curling antennae of the butterfly it would become.

The prince was astonished, and so was the scientific world when Swammerdam published his findings. The future creature had been there all along, hidden and unfinished, growing quietly inside the one that crawled. Modern biology has filled in the picture. Inside a caterpillar are small clusters of cells called imaginal discs, present from very early in its life, each carrying the plan for a wing or an eye or a leg. In the chrysalis much of the old body breaks down, and those discs draw on it to build the adult. Scientists still call the finished insect the imago, the Latin word for an image. Any Filipino child who has watched a fat green uod on a calamansi leaf and come back weeks later to find a swallowtail drying its wings has seen the miracle from the outside. Swammerdam was among the first to show it from within.

The apostle John, writing near the end of the first century, had a group of frightened believers who needed to see something like that about themselves. Tradition places him in Ephesus, an old man by then, the last living disciple who had leaned against Jesus at supper. The churches he loved had just been torn apart. A group of members had walked out, very likely taking friends and family with them, claiming they had moved on to a higher, more spiritual knowledge. They denied that Jesus was truly the Christ come in the flesh (1 John 2:22). John's verdict on their departure is blunt: "They went out from us, but they did not really belong to us. For if they had belonged to us, they would have remained with us" (1 John 2:19).

Picture the people left behind. They would have looked at the empty places on the benches where their house church met and wondered whether they were the foolish ones. The people who left had sounded so confident, so advanced. Those who stayed were ordinary believers who still struggled with temper and greed and doubt, and they may have quietly asked whether they belonged to God at all. So John, who keeps calling them "dear children," writes to steady them. He reminds them that they have "an anointing from the Holy One" (1 John 2:20), and he urges them to "continue in him, so that when he appears we may be confident and unashamed before him at his coming" (1 John 2:28). Then, as if he cannot hold it in any longer, he bursts out: "See what great love the Father has lavished on us, that we should be called children of God! And that is what we are!" (1 John 3:1).

"Dear friends, now we are children of God, and what we will be has not yet been made known. But we know that when Christ appears, we shall be like him, for we shall see him as he is." (1 John 3:2, NIV)

John holds two truths together in a single breath. The first is about the present: now we are children of God, fully and already, with nothing left to qualify for. The second is about the future: what we will be has not yet been made known. The Greek verb there, phaneroō, means to bring into the open, to make visible. John uses the very same word in the next clause for Christ's appearing. One way to read this is that our true selves are hidden in the same way Christ himself is hidden from the world for now, and that both will step into the light together on the same day. The finished child of God is already present, folded up inside the struggling believer, waiting for its unveiling.

Even the word John chose for the Father's love carries a note of wonder. The NIV renders it "great love," but the Greek potapēn originally meant something like "from what country?" It was the word you used for something so foreign and remarkable that you had to ask where on earth it came from. John is saying, in effect, that this love is from somewhere else entirely, and it has made strangers into sons and daughters.

A few verses later John adds an image that could have come straight out of Swammerdam's workroom. Explaining why a true child of God cannot settle comfortably into a life of sin, he writes that it is "because God's seed remains in them" (1 John 3:9). The word is sperma, the seed that carries a father's life and likeness into his child. John's point in that section is serious: those who belong to God do not make peace with doing wrong, and he wants his readers to take holiness seriously. Yet the ground of his confidence is gentle. Something of God's own life has been planted in you, and like those tiny clusters of cells in the caterpillar, it is steadily working toward the finished image. The Bible's story began with humanity made "in the image of God" (Genesis 1:27), and Paul describes believers as "being transformed into his image with ever-increasing glory" (2 Corinthians 3:18). John simply tells us where that road ends: "we shall be like him."

This matters on the ordinary mornings when you look at yourself honestly and do not like what you see. Perhaps you snapped at your children again, or the old habit you swore off came back, or your prayers feel as dry as a Bohol rice field in an El Niño summer. It is easy, on days like that, to conclude that God must be disappointed, or that real Christians are somehow made of different stuff. John would gently tell you that you are looking at the caterpillar and forgetting what is folded inside. A chrysalis looks like nothing is happening, and from the outside it can even look like decay, yet within it the future is being built with remarkable precision. What God will make of you is already folded inside you, and he has never once lost track of it.

That hope is meant to change how we live today, and John says so directly: "All who have this hope in him purify themselves, just as he is pure" (1 John 3:3). People who know what they are becoming begin to live toward it. A student who knows she will be a nurse starts washing her hands like one long before graduation. In the same way, a believer who knows she will one day be like Christ can begin, in small and faithful choices, to practice that likeness now, by apologizing first, by telling the truth when a small lie would be easier, and by forgiving the relative who has not asked for it. None of this earns the family name. It is simply what children who carry their Father's seed begin to do.

Before you leave for work or school today, consider writing four words from 1 John 3:1 on a slip of paper and tucking it into your wallet or taping it beside the mirror: "And that is what we are!" Read it when you have failed, and read it when you feel left behind by people who seem more spiritual than you. The Father who lavished this love on you does not wait until you are finished to call you his child. He calls you his child now, and one day, when Christ appears and you see him as he is, the wings that have been folded inside you all this time will finally open in the light.

articles.title: The King Who Could Not Sleep
articles.dek: Darius signed the law that sent Daniel to the lions, then spent the whole night awake. What he learned about God came from years of watching one faithful friend.
articles.quote: Faithfulness kept long enough becomes a language that even a king can learn to read.
articles.body:
Every year in classrooms across Japan, thirteen- and fourteen-year-olds open their Japanese language textbooks to a short story first published in 1940. It is called Hashire Merosu, or "Run, Melos!", and its author, Osamu Dazai, built it on an old Greek legend that the German poet Friedrich Schiller had once turned into a ballad. Many Japanese adults can still recite its famous first line, which simply says that Melos was enraged. Over the decades it has become the story a whole nation uses to teach its children what a true friend looks like.

The plot is simple. A shepherd named Melos walks into a city ruled by a king who trusts no one and has begun executing even members of his own family. Melos is arrested for daring to confront him and is sentenced to death, but he begs for three days to go home and see his younger sister married. The king laughs and agrees on one condition: Melos must leave his oldest friend, a stonemason named Selinuntius, as a hostage, and if Melos is not back by sunset on the third day, the friend will die in his place. The king is certain Melos will never return, and that the whole arrangement will prove what he already believes about people.

Melos goes home, the wedding takes place, and then the road back turns against him. A flood has washed out the bridge, bandits block the mountain pass, and the heat leaves him collapsed by the roadside, half-persuaded to give up. He gets up anyway and runs, arriving just as the sun goes down and his friend is already being bound for execution. The two men confess that each of them doubted the other for one moment, and they strike each other on the cheek as an act of honesty before they embrace. Then the tyrant, who has watched everything, comes down from his place and asks something nobody expected. He asks whether he may be their friend too.

A Filipino reader understands this story at once. We know the weight of a promise kept, the old palabra de honor, and we know the kind of barkada (circle of close friends) who would stand in your place if it ever came to that. Yet the character who moves readers most is the king, because hard hearts are usually won by watching someone stay faithful when it costs them. That is exactly what happens in Daniel 6.

The chapter opens just after one of the most famous nights in ancient history. Daniel 5 ends with Babylon falling to the Medes and Persians in a single night in 539 BC, while King Belshazzar feasted using the gold cups taken from the Jerusalem temple (Daniel 5:30). Daniel, now an old man who had been carried into exile as a teenager more than sixty years earlier, survives the change of empire. The new ruler, Darius the Mede, notices him almost at once and plans "to set him over the whole kingdom" (Daniel 6:3). The book of Daniel was treasured by exiles, people trying to stay faithful to God while serving inside a foreign system, and this chapter reads as though it were written with them in mind.

Daniel's jealous rivals search for something to use against him and come up empty. "They could not find any corruption in him, because he was trustworthy and neither corrupt nor negligent" (Daniel 6:4). Their only remaining option is to make his faith illegal, so they flatter Darius into signing a thirty-day decree forbidding prayer to any god or human except the king. Under Persian custom, a signed royal law could not be revoked (Daniel 6:8; compare Esther 8:8). When Daniel hears of it, he goes home to his upstairs room, where the windows open toward Jerusalem, and "three times a day he got down on his knees and prayed, giving thanks to his God, just as he had done before" (Daniel 6:10).

The trap closes, and at this point the chapter turns its attention to the king. "When the king heard this, he was greatly distressed; he was determined to rescue Daniel and made every effort until sundown to save him" (Daniel 6:14). He cannot undo his own law, and as Daniel is thrown into the den, Darius calls out to him, "May your God, whom you serve continually, rescue you!" (Daniel 6:16). Then he returns to his palace and spends the night without eating and without entertainment, and he cannot sleep (Daniel 6:18). At the first light of dawn he hurries back to the den.

"When he came near the den, he called to Daniel in an anguished voice, 'Daniel, servant of the living God, has your God, whom you serve continually, been able to rescue you from the lions?' Daniel answered, 'May the king live forever! My God sent his angel, and he shut the mouths of the lions. They have not hurt me, because I was found innocent in his sight. Nor have I ever done any wrong before you, Your Majesty.'" (Daniel 6:20–22)

One small word carries the whole relationship between these two men. Daniel 6 is part of the section of the book written in Aramaic, the shared language of the empire, and the word translated "continually" is bitdira, meaning constantly or without interruption. It appears only twice in the entire Bible, and both times it comes from the mouth of Darius (Daniel 6:16, 20). The king had no theology to speak of, but he had years of watching a man who kept showing up in the same way, at his desk by day and at his window in prayer. Faithfulness kept long enough becomes a language that even a king can learn to read.

The second thing worth seeing is Daniel's first sentence from the pit. The man who signed his death warrant is standing at the opening above him, and Daniel's opening words are a blessing: "May the king live forever!" He brings no accusation and no complaint about the long night he has just spent among lions because of a careless signature. One way to read this is that Daniel understood the king's heart better than the king's decree, and he chose to answer his friend's failure with grace. That grace is what turns the story outward, because by the end of the chapter Darius is writing to "all the nations and peoples of every language" that the God of Daniel "is the living God and he endures forever" (Daniel 6:25–26), much as Dazai's tyrant asked to join the friends he had tried to break.

Centuries later, the apostle Peter wrote to scattered Christians who were outsiders in their own neighborhoods, and his counsel sounds like a summary of Daniel's life: "Live such good lives among the pagans that, though they accuse you of doing wrong, they may see your good deeds and glorify God on the day he visits us" (1 Peter 2:12). Daniel lived that verse six hundred years before it was written. His enemies accused him while his king watched him, and in the end the watching proved stronger than the accusations.

Most of us have a Darius somewhere in our lives. It may be a manager who is decent but distant, or a relative who does not share your faith and once failed to stand up for you when it mattered. Such people may never sit through a sermon or open a Bible, yet they are quietly learning about God from the ordinary pattern of your days and from the way you treat them after they have let you down. That second lesson may be the one that reaches them, because it is the moment when grace becomes something they can actually see.

You might take a few minutes today to ask who has been watching your life without saying so, and what they have learned about God from your ordinary Tuesdays. If someone has disappointed you recently, perhaps a coworker who stayed silent or a family member who chose the easier side, consider letting your first words to them be a blessing, and allow the rest of the conversation to follow from there.

Kneeling at that window, Daniel had no idea that a king would one day lose sleep over him. He simply prayed where he had prayed the day before and trusted God with the rest. Your small, steady faithfulness is being read by someone right now, and the God who shut the mouths of the lions is fully able to use it to open a heart.

articles.title: The House He Wanted to Live In
articles.dek: David promised God a place to rest. Psalm 132 records God's reply, and he answers like a parent who was waiting for his child the whole time.
articles.quote: The God who could live anywhere looked at a small hill crowded with tired, ordinary people and said, I want to be here.
articles.body:
Many Filipino families know some version of this story. A son leaves his province for work in Dubai or Riyadh, and for nine years most of his salary goes home. He sends money for tuition, for medicine, and finally for a house. He wants his mother to have hollow blocks instead of old wood, a real roof that the typhoons cannot peel back, and a tiled kitchen where she will never again have to set out a basin when it rains. On video calls he watches the walls go up one course at a time. He tells himself that when it is finished, she will finally be able to rest.

When he comes home for good, the house is beautiful. His mother walks him through every room, proud of the paint and the new gate. Then she takes him into the one room she never changed, his old bedroom, with the same faded curtain and the same narrow bed, and she sets a bowl of sinigang in front of him because she has been cooking it in her head for nine years. "Maganda ang bahay, anak," she tells him. "Pero ikaw ang hinihintay ko." The house is lovely, but you are the one I was waiting for. He had spent years building her a place to rest, and he finds out that her rest was always going to be his coming home.

Psalm 132 carries that same surprise, and it lands on a whole nation.

The psalm belongs to the Songs of Ascents (Psalms 120 to 134), which pilgrims sang as they climbed the roads up to Jerusalem for the great feasts. Families walked for days with children on their shoulders, and somewhere on the climb they would sing this song about King David and the ark of the covenant. The ark was the gold-covered chest that held the tablets of the law, the sign of God's presence among his people. For years it had been neglected in a small town called Kiriath Jearim. Then David brought it up to Jerusalem with music and dancing (2 Samuel 6).

The first half of the psalm remembers David's devotion. "LORD, remember David and all his self-denial" (Psalm 132:1). It recalls an oath David made: "I will not enter my house or go to my bed, I will allow no sleep to my eyes or slumber to my eyelids, till I find a place for the LORD, a dwelling for the Mighty One of Jacob" (Psalm 132:3–5). David was the son working abroad, so to speak, refusing his own comfort until God had a proper home. The pilgrims then pray on his behalf: "Arise, LORD, and come to your resting place, you and the ark of your might" (Psalm 132:8).

Then, at verse 11, the speaker changes. David swore an oath to God, and now "the LORD swore an oath to David, a sure oath he will not revoke" (Psalm 132:11). God answers with a promise of his own, and at the center of it he says this:

"This is my resting place for ever and ever; here I will sit enthroned, for I have desired it." (Psalm 132:14, NIV)

The Hebrew word for "resting place" is menuchah, the same family of words used for the settled rest God gave Israel when the wandering in the wilderness was over. It describes a place where you put down your bags and stay. The word translated "desired" is even warmer. It comes from the Hebrew verb 'avah, which elsewhere describes a real craving, the kind of longing a hungry person has for food. Verse 13 uses it first ("he has desired it for his dwelling"), and verse 14 repeats it so the point cannot be missed. God tells his people that he chose Zion because he wanted to live there.

Zion was a small ridge in a small country, and most of the people who lived on it were farmers, shepherds, and day laborers. The God who could live anywhere looked at a small hill crowded with tired, ordinary people and said, I want to be here. Read alongside 2 Samuel 7, this becomes even more tender. When David first offered to build God a house, God gently replied through the prophet Nathan that he would build a house for David, a family line that would last (2 Samuel 7:11). Psalm 132 sings the same reversal. David worked to give God a home, and God answered by making a home for David and for everyone who would gather there.

One way to read the rest of God's oath is to set it beside the pilgrims' prayer in verses 8 and 9, because God answers that prayer line by line and gives more each time. The people asked, "May your priests be clothed with your righteousness" (Psalm 132:9). God replies, "I will clothe her priests with salvation" (Psalm 132:16). They prayed that the faithful would "sing for joy" (Psalm 132:9). God promises that they "will ever sing for joy" (Psalm 132:16), and the Hebrew there doubles the verb, something like "they will shout and shout for joy." Then he adds gifts nobody asked for: "I will bless her with abundant provisions; her poor I will satisfy with food" (Psalm 132:15), and "here I will make a horn grow for David and set up a lamp for my anointed one" (Psalm 132:17). A horn was an image of strength, and a lamp in a house meant someone was still living there. God was promising that David's line would never go dark, a promise the New Testament sees fulfilled in Jesus, the Son of David, of whom John writes that "the Word became flesh and made his dwelling among us" (John 1:14).

Like the son in Dubai, many of us approach God as though our main job is to prepare a place worthy of him. We tidy our lives before we pray. We assume he will come close once we have read more, served more, or finally stopped struggling with the same weakness. Effort has its place; David's devotion is honored in this very psalm. Still, the psalm ends with God's oath, and that oath says he chose his people's company before they finished building anything. The poor in verse 15 are fed because God moved in among them, and the priests are dressed in salvation because God chose to sit enthroned in their midst.

This may be the word you need if you are coming to the end of this week tired. Perhaps the bills ran ahead of the paycheck, or a parent's health has you sleeping lightly, or you have simply carried more than anyone can see. You may feel that your heart is a house with a leaking roof and that God surely has better places to be. Psalm 132 suggests that the God of the pilgrims looks at your weary life and says, with the same longing a mother feels for a returning child, that he wants to be there.

Before you sleep tonight, you might try a very simple prayer. Sit for five quiet minutes, without performing and without first fixing anything, and tell God one plain, honest thing about your day. Then read Psalm 132:14 aloud and receive it as spoken over you: "This is my resting place for ever and ever; here I will sit enthroned, for I have desired it." If you made a request this week, hold it with open hands, remembering that the God of this psalm has a habit of answering with salvation when we only asked for righteousness, and with shouting joy when we asked to sing.

The pilgrims sang this song as they climbed, with sore feet and dusty clothes, and they sang it before they ever reached the temple gates. They did not have to arrive polished to be wanted. Neither do you. The house he wants to live in is the one with you in it, and the light he promised to keep burning is still on.

articles.title: The Table Where Gossip Starved
articles.dek: Augustine carved a warning into his dining table, and Proverbs explains why it worked: a quarrel needs someone to keep feeding it. The fire stops when one person stops adding wood.
articles.quote: You may not be able to put out every fire in your family or your office, but you can always refuse to be its wood.
articles.body:
In the North African port town of Hippo, sometime around the year 400, a bishop had two lines of Latin verse inscribed on his dining table. Guests came to that table often, because the bishop was Augustine, one of the most respected minds of his age, and his house was full of clergy, travelers, and friends. The verse read, in plain English: Whoever loves to gnaw at the lives of absent people with his words should know that this table is not worthy of him. His friend and biographer Possidius, who ate at that table for nearly forty years, recorded the inscription and added a small, telling story. Once, when some fellow bishops forgot the warning and began to pick apart someone who was not in the room, Augustine grew stern. Either those lines would have to be scratched off the table, he told them, or he would get up and leave in the middle of the meal.

Augustine wrote enormous books on grace, time, and the city of God, yet one of the most practical things he ever did was decide what would and would not be served at dinner. He understood that gossip is a kind of food, passed around and enjoyed in company, and that a host can decide to stop serving it. Long before him, a wise man in Israel had seen the very same thing.

Proverbs 26 belongs to a collection of sayings that, according to Proverbs 25:1, were "compiled by the men of Hezekiah king of Judah." These were court scribes, copying out Solomon's wisdom for a nation that needed it. The chapter is a gallery of people who wreck community: the fool, the sluggard, the meddler. Then, in verses 18 to 23, the writer turns to the damage done by the mouth. He describes a man who is "like a maniac shooting flaming arrows of death" and then shrugs and says, "I was only joking!" (Prov 26:18–19). He describes "a quarrelsome person" who is to strife what "charcoal to embers and as wood to fire" are to a blaze (Prov 26:21). In the middle of all that smoke sits one calm, almost hopeful sentence.

"Without wood a fire goes out; without a gossip a quarrel dies down." (Proverbs 26:20, NIV)

The Hebrew word translated "gossip" here is nirgan, which carries the sense of a whisperer, someone who murmurs things quietly from one ear to the next. It is the same word used in Proverbs 16:28, where "a gossip separates close friends." The whisperer rarely starts the original conflict. A misunderstanding happens, a sharp word is spoken, someone feels slighted. That is the spark. The whisperer is the one who keeps carrying sticks to it, retelling the story, adding a detail, asking a friend, "Did you hear what she said about you?"

Then verse 22 explains why so many of us find this hard to resist: "The words of a gossip are like choice morsels; they go down to the inmost parts." The Hebrew for "choice morsels" comes from a root that suggests something gulped down greedily, a treat you swallow before you have even thought about it. The phrase "inmost parts" is literally "the chambers of the belly." Gossip tastes good, and once it is swallowed it stays inside us. It shapes how we look at a coworker on Monday morning, or how we greet a cousin at the next family reunion. This is exactly why Augustine's table imagery fits so well. The proverb itself pictures gossip as something eaten, and he simply took the dish off the menu.

One way to read verse 20 is as a word of real hope. Fire is frightening because it seems to have a life of its own, yet every fire depends on fuel. Take away the wood and the most furious blaze settles into ash. The writer is telling us that most quarrels are kept alive by something, and that the "something" is often a person. That means one person can also end it. You may not be able to put out every fire in your family or your office, but you can always refuse to be its wood. That is a modest kind of power, and it is available to anyone, including the quietest person in the group chat.

Filipinos know this fire well. We have a playful name for the neighbor who knows everyone's business, and we laugh about the tsismis that travels faster than the tricycle from the sari-sari store to the chapel. Much of it feels harmless, a way of staying connected. But Proverbs warns that the whisperer can be as dangerous as the man with flaming arrows, and that the excuse "I was only joking" does not unburn anything. Centuries later James would say the same thing in his own words: "Consider what a great forest is set on fire by a small spark" (James 3:5). A forwarded screenshot, a raised eyebrow over merienda, a sentence that begins with "Don't tell anyone, but" can each become that spark.

The gospel gives this proverb its deepest meaning. Scripture calls the devil "the accuser of our brothers and sisters, who accuses them before our God day and night" (Rev 12:10). The Greek word for devil, diabolos, means slanderer. At the very heart of evil is a voice that talks about people behind their backs. Jesus is the opposite. Paul writes, "Who then is the one who condemns? No one. Christ Jesus who died, more than that, who was raised to life, is at the right hand of God and is also interceding for us" (Rom 8:34). Right now, in the presence of God, the One who knows every one of your failures is speaking about you, and what he says is said in your defense. He knows the full story of your worst moments, and he covers them with his own blood.

When we grasp that, gossip starts to lose its taste. We stop needing to feel bigger by making someone else smaller, because we have already been lifted up by grace. Proverbs 17:9 puts the choice in front of us: "Whoever would foster love covers over an offense, but whoever repeats the matter separates close friends." A Christian who has been covered by Christ becomes, almost naturally, someone who covers others. This does not mean hiding abuse or ignoring wrongdoing that must be addressed. It means bringing hard matters to the person involved, or to those who can help, instead of feeding them to an audience.

There is a gentle practice hidden in Augustine's table. You could choose one setting this week, perhaps your family's dinner table, your office pantry, or a group chat, and quietly decide that absent people will be safe there. When the conversation turns toward someone who is not present, you might say something kind about them, ask a question that changes the subject, or simply decline to add your own stick. Most of the time no one will notice, which is fine. Proverbs promises that without wood the fire goes out, and you will find that many quarrels die down simply because one person stopped feeding them.

Verse 23 ends this passage with a final picture: "Like a coating of silver dross on earthenware are fervent lips with an evil heart." A cheap clay pot can be glazed to look like silver, yet it remains clay underneath. Our words reveal what our hearts are made of, and the good news is that God makes new hearts. The same Lord who speaks well of you before the Father can teach your mouth to speak well of others. Today, let your table be a place where the absent are protected, and let your words carry the same grace that has been spoken over you.
